extracted.intended_audience: scholars and students of journalism/media studies, newsroom managers, and journalists interested in editorial policy and newsworthiness
extracted.subtask_description: Analyzing how implicit newsroom policy and socialization determine what is pursued, emphasized, or buried as news; summarizes mechanisms by which reporters learn and conform to an outlet's covert policy and the implications for newsworthiness. Useful for evaluating newsroom practices and predicting systematic biases in coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reading their own paper
rubrics_metrics.description: New reporters infer policy from the paper's existing coverage patterns.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicitly learning what angles, beats, and story types are acceptable by observing what the outlet publishes; used as a primary socialization mechanism rather than formal instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial blue-pencil
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct edits and deletions by editors communicate the boundaries of acceptable coverage; reporters learn limits by observing what is modified or removed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conferences and gossip
rubrics_metrics.description: Watercooler talk transmits taboos and preferred frames.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal conversations, editorial conferences, and workplace gossip circulate tacit norms and warnings about what to avoid or emphasize (taboos, preferred framings).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipatory self-censorship
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters internalize policy and avoid filing stories likely to be killed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters preemptively shape or withhold coverage based on expectations of editorial reaction, reducing direct conflict and producing conformity without explicit orders.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional authority and sanctions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Formal positional power (assignments, hiring/firing) creates strong incentives to conform; authority and potential sanctions enforce editorial policy even when unwritten.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feelings of obligation and esteem for superiors
rubrics_metrics.description: Personal loyalty to mentors encourages conformity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emotional bonds and respect for editors and senior reporters (esteem/obligation) motivate reporters to align with perceived preferences and protect reputational ties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mobility aspirations
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambitions for promotion or movement within the profession encourage conformity to outlet norms as a strategic career behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Absence of conflicting group allegiance
rubrics_metrics.description: No counter-organization (weak unions in 1950s) to back deviance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When reporters lack alternative organizational protections or collective backing, individual deviance is riskier and less likely; weak countervailing groups increase conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: The pleasant nature of the activity
rubrics_metrics.description: Reporters enjoy the job and avoid disrupting it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intrinsic job satisfaction and desire to preserve a congenial work environment reduce incentive to challenge policy; people avoid actions that would jeopardize enjoyable work routines.

rubrics_metrics.name: News as a value in itself
rubrics_metrics.description: Getting the story trumps fighting policy battles.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commitment to producing news (the scoop/value of reporting) leads reporters to prioritize publishing and pursuing stories within accepted channels rather than confronting policy conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Norms of policy are not always defined (ambiguity creates discretion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity in norms provides reporters discretion to bypass policy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When expectations are vague or inconsistently applied, reporters can interpret situations in ways that allow deviation from covert policy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Executives sometimes ignorant of facts
rubrics_metrics.description: Executives' lack of knowledge about particulars allows reporters to finesse coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reporters can exploit editors' factual ignorance to frame or present stories that might otherwise be curtailed if higher-ups were fully informed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plant the story with a wire service
rubrics_metrics.description: Use external publication to force editors to run a story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tactic for bypassing local editorial control: have the story appear on a wire so editors face pressure to carry it, reducing their ability to suppress coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Star reporters have leverage
rubrics_metrics.guidance: High-profile reporters gain bargaining power to pursue atypical stories or angles because their name or draw reduces editors' willingness to restrain them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reporters with strong policy convictions
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Individual reporters who strongly believe in a story or principle may occasionally overcome newsroom resistance, particularly when combining persistence with strategy or leverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy as covert prior (unwritten newsworthiness filter)
rubrics_metrics.description: Outlet policy operates as an unwritten newsworthiness filter — what counts as a story differs systematically by paper because of socialization, not just market.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Newsworthiness is conditioned by tacit, outlet-specific norms learned through socialization; two papers may treat the same event differently because of their covert priors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conservatism bias (protection of property and class interests)
rubrics_metrics.description: Policy 'usually protects property and class interests' — important information may be slanted, buried, or denied to citizenry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit editorial policies tend to favor established interests, producing systematic biases (e.g., suppressing or softening stories that challenge property/class norms).

rubrics_metrics.name: Newsroom socialization > formal rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Conformity is achieved without explicit instruction; tacit norms learned through immersion override formal rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Informal socialization mechanisms (observation, gossip, editing practices) are often more powerful than written policies in shaping coverage decisions and reporter behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: High morale leads to policy compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: When reporters feel part of the team, policy conflicts are shelved in favor of 'getting more news.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Strong group cohesion and high morale reduce challenges to editorial policy, as reporters prioritize group goals and smooth operations over internal dissent.
